•Company secured $13.2 billion in cash proceeds from the Kenvue debt offering and initial public offering and maintains 9.5%
of equity stake in Kenvue
•Company maintains its quarterly dividend of $1.19 per share
New Brunswick, N.J. (August 30, 2023) – Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) (“the Company”) today announced updates to its financials and
2023 guidance which reflect its operations as a company focused on transformational innovation in Pharmaceutical and MedTech. The
Company has published a recorded webinar for investors to provide additional context behind the updated financials and 2023 guidance
found in this release, which may be accessed by visiting the Investors section of the Company's website at webcasts & presentations.
“The completion of this transaction uniquely positions Johnson & Johnson as a Pharmaceutical and MedTech company focused on delivering
transformative healthcare solutions to patients,” said Joaquin Duato, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer. “We are incredibly
proud of the focus and dedication of our employees worldwide to achieve this milestone, which we are confident will unlock near- and long-
term value for all of our stakeholders.”
As previously announced, the Company recently completed an exchange offer to finalize the separation of Kenvue Inc., formerly Johnson &
Johnson’s Consumer Health business. As a result of the completion of the exchange offer, Johnson & Johnson will now present its
Consumer Health business financial results as discontinued operations, including a gain of approximately $20 billion in the third quarter of
2023.
Unless otherwise noted, the financial results and earnings guidance included below have been recast to reflect the continuing operations of
Johnson & Johnson.

top1_chunks.summary:
- Scope: Corporate segment of JPMorgan Chase; references pages 83–84 of the 2020 Form 10-K. Presents selected income statement, balance sheet data, and commentary for the three months ended March 31, 2021 vs. 2020.
- Results: Net loss widened to $580M from $125M; total net revenue was a loss of $473M vs. a gain of $166M.
- Revenue mix:
  - Net interest income fell sharply to $(855)M (from $(165)M) due to lower rates and limited opportunities to deploy excess deposits.
  - Noninterest revenue rose 15% to $382M, with principal transactions swinging to a $272M gain (from a $(113)M loss), partly offset by a 94% drop in investment securities gains ($14M vs. $233M) reflecting investment securities portfolio repositioning and lower gains on certain Corporate investments; “all other income” declined 55%.
  - Includes tax-equivalent adjustments of $67M (2021) and $61M (2020).
- Expenses and credit:
  - Noninterest expense increased 500% to $876M, driven by a higher contribution to the Firm’s Foundation and higher structural expenses.
  - Provision for credit losses was $16M vs. $8M.
- Taxes: Current-period income tax benefit driven by the change in level/mix of income and expenses across tax jurisdictions and the full-year expected tax rate relative to year-to-date pretax income, partially offset by resolutions of certain tax audits.
- Segment detail:
  - Treasury and CIO: total net revenue $(705)M (vs. $169M); net loss $(675)M (vs. $83M income).
  - Other Corporate: total net revenue $232M (vs. $(3)M); net income $95M (vs. $(208)M loss).
- Balance sheet and headcount: Total assets up 44% to $1.41T; loans down 1% to $1.627B; headcount down 2% to 38,168.

top5_chunks.title: Revenue
top5_chunks.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three months ended March 31, 2021 vs. 2020, with cross-references to segment details and critical accounting estimates.
- Total net revenue: Up 14% to $32.3B, driven by a 40% increase in noninterest revenue; net interest income declined 11%.
- Investment banking fees: Up 59% to $3.0B, reflecting stronger equity underwriting (IPOs), increased advisory from more completed deals, and higher debt underwriting (high-yield and leveraged loans) amid higher industry fees and wallet share gains (CIB).
- Principal transactions revenue: Up 121% to $6.5B, aided by absence of two large prior-year losses (CIB Credit Adjustments & Other and bridge financing markdowns). Excluding these, growth came from strong Equity Markets (derivatives, cash equities, prime brokerage) and Fixed Income Markets (securitized products, credit), partly offset by lower Rates and Currencies & EM; also net gains on legacy private equity in Corporate. Note that CIB Markets performance is assessed on total revenue, given offsets with net interest income.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 1%, as lower deposit-related fees in CCB (from higher balances) were largely offset by higher cash management fees in CIB/CB and higher lending-related/commitment fees in CIB.
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Up 11% to $5.0B, driven by higher AWM fees from strong net inflows into long-term and liquidity products and higher market levels (net of liquidity fee waivers), plus higher investment assets in CCB.
- Investment securities gains: Down 94% to $14MM, reflecting portfolio repositioning.
- Mortgage fees and related income: Up 120% to $704MM on higher production margins and volumes (CCB).
- Card income: Up 36% to $1.35B on lower acquisition costs and higher net interchange as debit/credit spend returned to pre-pandemic levels (CCB).
- Other income: Down 10% to $1.12B, due to weather-related write-downs and higher amortization in tax-oriented renewable energy investments (offset in part by related tax credits), lower gains on certain Corporate investments, and lower auto operating lease income in CCB; partially offset by valuation gains in AWM and the absence of prior-year losses on certain CIB equity investments. Footnote notes operating lease income of $1.3B (2021) vs. $1.4B (2020).
- Net interest income: Down 11% to $12.9B, predominantly from lower rates, partly offset by balance sheet growth. Average interest-earning assets rose $661B to $3.1T; yield fell 127 bps to 1.87%. Net yield (FTE) fell 68 bps to 1.69%; excluding CIB Markets, net yield fell 108 bps to 1.93% (non-GAAP measures referenced).
- Provision for credit losses: Swing to a net release of $4.16B vs. an $8.29B build in prior year, driven by reductions in both consumer and wholesale allowances.
  - Consumer: $3.50B net release vs. $5.68B build, reflecting a $4.5B allowance reduction (including $3.5B in Card from improved macroeconomic scenarios and $625MM in Home Lending from improved HPI and portfolio runoff), lower Card net charge-offs helped by payment assistance and government stimulus, and comparison to a $4.4B prior-year build.
  - Wholesale: $671MM net release vs. $2.59B build, reflecting a $716MM allowance reduction on improved macroeconomic scenarios.
- Repeated references to segment-level discussions (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate) and notes for further detail, including non-GAAP reconciliations and credit allowance disclosures.

Negative effects on JPMorgan Chase include reduced demand and higher allowance for credit losses, with heightened model risk in estimating credit losses. Potential further impacts: increased credit losses, asset valuation declines, ratings downgrades, liquidity/capital constraints (e.g., elevated deposits, higher RWA, client rating downgrades, regulatory actions), and workforce disruptions. The severity and duration are uncertain and depend on pandemic trajectory, vaccine effectiveness, and government actions; stimulus and payment assistance may delay charge-offs. Participation in government support programs could increase scrutiny, litigation risk, costs, and reputational harm, and may amplify other existing risks.

top5_chunks.text:
Item 1A. Risk Factors.
The following discussion supplements the discussion of risk
factors affecting the Firm as set forth in Part I, Item 1A:
Risk Factors on pages 8-32  of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2020  Form 
10-K . The discussion of risk factors, as so supplemented, 
sets forth the material risk factors that could affect 
JPMorgan Chase’s financial condition and operations. 
Readers should not consider any descriptions of such 
factors to be a complete set of all potential risks that could 
affect the Firm.
The COVID-19 pandemic has caused and is causing 
significant harm to the global economy and could further 
negatively affect certain of JPMorgan Chase’s businesses. 
On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization 
declared the outbreak of a strain of novel coronavirus 
disease, COVID-19, to be a global pandemic. The COVID-19 
pandemic and governmental responses to the pandemic led 
to the institution of social distancing and shelter-in-place 
requirements in certain areas of the U.S. and other 
countries resulting in ongoing severe impacts on global 
economic conditions, including:
• significant disruption and volatility in the financial 
markets 
• significant disruption of global supply chains, and 
• closures of many businesses, leading to loss of 
revenues and increased unemployment.  
A prolongation or worsening of the pandemic, or the 
emergence of other diseases that give rise to similar 
effects, could deepen the adverse impact on the global 
economy. 
The adverse economic conditions caused by the pandemic 
have had a negative impact on certain of JPMorgan Chase’s 
businesses and results of operations, including:
• reduction in demand for certain products and services 
from JPMorgan Chase’s clients and customers, resulting 
in lower revenue, and
• increases in the allowance for credit losses.
Certain models used by JPMorgan Chase in connection with 
the determination of the allowance for credit losses have 
heightened performance risk in the economic environment 
precipitated by the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and 
government stimulus. There can be no assurance that, even 
after adjustments have been made to model outputs, 
JPMorgan Chase will not recognize unexpected losses 
arising from the model uncertainty that has resulted from 
these developments. 
172A prolongation or worsening of the COVID-19 pandemic and 
the negative economic impacts of the pandemic could have 
other significant adverse effects on JPMorgan Chase’s 
businesses, results of operations and financial condition, 
including:
• recognition of credit losses and further increases in the 
allowance for credit losses, especially to the extent that 
businesses remain closed, unemployment continues at 
elevated levels, clients and customers draw on their 
lines of credit or significant numbers of people relocate 
from metropolitan areas
• material impacts on the value of securities, derivatives 
and other financial instruments which JPMorgan Chase 
owns or in which it makes markets
• downgrades in JPMorgan Chase’s credit ratings
• constraints on liquidity or capital due to elevated levels 
of deposits, increases in risk-weighted assets (“RWA”) 
related to supporting client activities, downgrades in 
client credit ratings, regulatory actions or other factors, 
any or all of which could require JPMorgan Chase to 
take or refrain from taking actions that it otherwise 
would under its liquidity and capital management 
strategies, and
• the possibility that significant portions of JPMorgan 
Chase’s workforce are unable to work effectively, 
including because of illness, quarantines, shelter-in-
place arrangements, government actions or other 
restrictions in connection with the pandemic.
The extent to which the COVID-19 pandemic negatively 
affects JPMorgan Chase’s businesses, results of operations 
and financial condition, as well as its regulatory capital and 
liquidity ratios, will depend on future developments that are 
highly uncertain and cannot be predicted, including the 
ultimate scope and duration of the pandemic, the 
effectiveness of vaccination programs and actions taken by 
governmental authorities and other third parties in 
response to the pandemic. Those negative effects, including 
the possible recognition of charge-offs, may be delayed because of the impact of prior and potential future 
government stimulus actions or payment assistance 
provided to clients and customers. 
In addition, JPMorgan Chase’s participation directly or 
indirectly, including on behalf of customers and clients or 
by affiliated entities, in U.S. government programs designed 
to support individuals, households and businesses impacted 
by the economic disruptions caused by the COVID-19 
pandemic could be criticized and subject JPMorgan Chase 
to:
• increased governmental and regulatory scrutiny
• negative publicity, and 
• increased exposure to litigation, 
any or all of which could increase JPMorgan Chase’s 
operational, legal and compliance costs and damage its 
reputation. To the extent that the COVID-19 pandemic 
adversely affects JPMorgan Chase’s business, results of 
operations and financial condition, it may also have the 
effect of heightening many of the other risks described in 
Risk Factors in the 2020 Form 10-K. 
Supervision and regulation
Refer to the Supervision and regulation section on pages 3–
7 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020  Form 10-K for information on 
Supervision and Regulation.

- Scale and growth:
  - Total assets rose to $3.689T from $3.385T; total liabilities rose to $3.409T from $3.105T; total stockholders’ equity increased to $280.7B from $279.4B.
- Key asset movements:
  - Large increase in deposits with banks ($685.7B vs. $502.7B).
  - Trading assets up ($544.1B vs. $503.1B) and securities borrowed up.
  - Investment securities net relatively stable: AFS slightly lower, HTM higher.
  - Gross loans roughly flat (~$1.01T); allowance for loan losses decreased ($23.0B vs. $28.3B), lifting net loans.
  - Accrued interest and receivables, and other assets, increased meaningfully.
  - Several categories include amounts at fair value and assets pledged.
- Key liability movements:
  - Customer deposits increased to $2.278T from $2.144T.
  - Higher federal funds purchased and repos; higher trading and other liabilities.
  - Long-term debt slightly decreased; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs declined.
- Consolidated VIEs:
  - Assets $36.2B and liabilities $15.9B at March 31, 2021 (down from $40.2B and $17.8B).
  - Beneficial interest holders generally have no recourse to JPMorgan; amounts exclude intercompany eliminations.

  - Net income of $14.3B; dividends declared: $2.76B common ($0.90/share) and $379M preferred.

  - Share repurchases of $5.0B and reissuances of $1.0B increased treasury stock (more negative).
  - Additional paid-in capital decreased due to share-based compensation effects.
  - Accumulated other comprehensive income fell by $6.9B; retained earnings rose to $248.2B.

top5_chunks.title: Revenue
top5_chunks.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three and six months ended June 30, 2023 vs. 2022; segment-specific drivers addressed in segment sections; references to critical accounting estimates and non-GAAP measures.

- Headline results:
  - Q2 2023: Noninterest revenue $19.5B (+25%); Net interest income (NII) $21.8B (+44%); Total net revenue $41.3B (+34%).
  - H1 2023: Noninterest revenue $37.2B (+15%); NII $42.5B (+47%); Total net revenue $79.7B (+30%).

- Quarterly (Q2 2023 vs. Q2 2022) revenue line drivers:
  - Investment banking fees: Down 5%; lower advisory amid weaker deal activity; largely offset by higher equity underwriting (more convertible and follow-on offerings as volatility eased).
  - Principal transactions: Up 38%; stronger Equity Markets (Prime Finance) and Fixed Income Markets (Securitized Products, Fixed Income Financing); absence of prior-year bridge financing markdowns; Credit Adjustments & Other swung to a gain; higher Treasury & CIO cash deployment revenue; partly offset by weaker Rates and Currencies & Emerging Markets and losses on legacy private equity in Corporate. Markets principal transactions gains were more than offset by lower Markets NII due to higher funding costs; performance is assessed on total net revenue.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 2%; lower cash management fees from higher client earnings credits; partly offset by higher lending-related fees tied to the First Republic acquisition in AWM and CCB.
  - Asset management fees: Up 7%; higher management fees on strong AWM net inflows and First Republic impact in CCB.
  - Commissions and other fees: Flat.
  - Investment securities losses: Larger losses from sales of U.S. Treasuries and agency MBS tied to portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO.
  - Mortgage fees and related income: Down 26%; lower production volumes and lower net servicing revenue.
  - Card income: Down 3%; higher rewards liability from program term changes reduced net interchange; partly offset by stronger Commercial Card in CIB and CB.
  - Other income: Up sharply (includes a $2.7B estimated bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition); also benefited from absence of prior-year Payments equity investment losses and net investment hedges in Treasury & CIO; partially offset by lower auto operating lease income and absence of a prior-year CB equity-method gain.

- Year-to-date (H1 2023 vs. H1 2022) revenue line drivers:
  - Investment banking fees: Down 12%; lower debt underwriting (weaker acquisition financing) and lower advisory; partly offset by higher equity underwriting (more convertibles and Q2 follow-ons).
  - Principal transactions: Up 44%; stronger Fixed Income (Securitized Products, Fixed Income Financing) and Equity Markets (Prime Finance); improved Credit Adjustments & Other vs. prior-year losses; higher Treasury & CIO cash deployment revenue; Markets principal transactions strength more than offset by lower Markets NII from higher funding costs.
  - Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 7%; lower cash management fees from higher client earnings credits; partly offset by First Republic-driven lending-related fees in AWM and CCB.
  - Asset management fees: Up 1%; increase driven by First Republic impact in CCB; AWM roughly flat as market declines were offset by fewer money fund fee waivers and net inflows.
  - Commissions and other fees: Flat.
  - Investment securities losses: Higher losses from sales of Treasuries and agency MBS as portfolios were repositioned in both periods in Treasury & CIO.
  - Mortgage fees and related income: Down 40%; lower production volumes and lower servicing revenue (including lower MSR risk management gains).
  - Card income: Up 10%; higher payments-related revenue (Commercial Card growth in CIB and CB); CCB net interchange roughly flat—Q1 partner payments benefit from a tax refund on airline miles offset by higher rewards liability from program changes.
  - Other income: Higher, driven by the $2.7B First Republic bargain purchase gain, net investment hedges in Treasury & CIO, and a $339M gain in AWM from stepping up its CIFM stake; partially offset by lower auto lease income, absence of prior-year insurance settlement and CB equity-method gain, and lower gains on certain Corporate investments.

- Net interest income and balance/yield metrics:
  - NII increased in both periods primarily from higher rates, with additional contributions from the First Republic acquisition (and higher revolving Card balances YTD); partially offset by lower Markets NII and lower average deposits.
  - Average interest-earning assets: $3.3T (Q2 down $42B; H1 down $113B).
  - Yield on interest-earning assets: 5.01% in Q2 (+279 bps); 4.85% YTD (+281 bps).
  - Net yield on these assets (FTE): 2.62% in Q2 (+82 bps); 2.63% YTD (+89 bps).
  - Net yield excluding Markets (non-GAAP): 3.83% in Q2 (+157 bps); 3.82% YTD (+171 bps).

- Notable one-time/transactional items:
  - Estimated $2.7B bargain purchase gain from the First Republic acquisition (recorded in Corporate) materially lifted Other income.
  - Investment securities portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO drove elevated realized losses.
  - Markets results show offsets between principal transactions and NII; firm evaluates Markets on total net revenue.

basis points (“bps”). The net yield on these assets, on an 
FTE basis, was 2.62%, an increase of 82 bps. The net yield 
excluding Markets was 3.83%, up 157 bps.

and rates schedule on page 198 for further information;  
and Business Segment Results on page 24  and Note 28 for additional information on the First Republic acquisition.
Net yield excluding Markets is a non-GAAP financial 
measure. Refer to Explanation and Reconciliation of the 
Firm’s Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures on pages 20-21  
for a further discussion of Net yield excluding Markets.
Year-to-date results
Investment banking fees  decreased in CIB, reflecting:
•lower debt underwriting fees as challenging market 
conditions resulted in lower issuance activity in 
acquisition financing , and
•lower advisory fees due to a lower level of announced 
deals in prior periods amid a challenging environment,  
partially offset by
•higher equity  underwriting fees primarily due to higher 
convertible securities offerings and, in the second half of 
the second quarter, follow-on offerings that benefited 
from the lower equity market volatility.
Principal transactions revenue  increased, reflecting:
•higher Fixed Income Markets net revenue in principal 
transactions,  driven by Securitized Products and Fixed 
Income Financing, partially offset by lower revenue in 
Currencies & Emerging Markets  and Rates ,
•higher Equity Markets revenue in principal transactions, 
primarily in Prime Finance,
–the increase in Markets principal transactions revenue 
was more than offset by a decline in Markets NII, 
primarily due to higher funding costs
•losses of $117 million in Credit Adjustments & Other in 
CIB, driven by losses on certain components of fair value 
option elected liabilities,  compared with losses of $742 
million in the prior year,  and
•higher revenue related to cash deployment transactions 
in Treasury and CIO.
Lending- and deposit-related fees  decr eased due to:
•lower cash management fees in CB and CIB associated 
with the higher level of credits earned by clients that 
reduce such fees,
partially offset by
•higher lending-related fees driven by the impact of the 
First Republic acquisition  in AWM and CCB .
Asset management fees  increased driven by the impact of 
the First Republic acquisition in CCB.
Asset management  fees in AWM was relatively flat, as the 
decline in market levels was predominantly offset by the 
removal of most money market fund fee waivers and the 
impact of net inflows.
Commissions  and other fees  was relatively flat. Refer to 
CIB and AWM segment results on pages 30-36  and pages 
41-44 , respectively, and Note 6 for additional information.
Investme nt securities losses  reflected higher net losses on 
sales of U.S. Treasuries and U.S. GSE and government 
agency MBS, associated with repositioning the investment 
securities portfolio in both periods in Treasury and CIO.
Mortgage fees and related income decreased driven by 
11Home Lending, reflecting lower production revenue due to a

top5_chunks.title: Selected income statement and balance sheet data
top5_chunks.summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase Corporate segment results, with reference to further background in the 2022 Form 10-K (pp. 79–80).
- Strong turnaround: Q2 2023 net income of $2.6 billion versus a net loss of $174 million in Q2 2022; year-to-date net income of $2.9 billion versus a $1.0 billion loss in the prior year.
- Revenue surge: Total net revenue of $3.7 billion in Q2 2023 versus $80 million a year ago; year-to-date $4.7 billion versus a loss in the prior year.
- Key drivers:
  - Higher net interest income from higher rates, partly offset by lower firmwide average deposit balances available for deployment in Treasury and CIO.
  - Noninterest revenue boosted by an estimated $2.7 billion bargain purchase gain related to the First Republic acquisition and higher Treasury and CIO cash deployment revenue.
  - Offsets included larger net investment securities losses from portfolio repositioning (sales of U.S. Treasuries and GSE/government agency MBS) and net losses on certain legacy private equity positions (versus gains in the prior year).
  - Comparatives benefited from larger prior-year losses tied to foreign exchange movements; FX also affected current-year revenue/expense where FX risk was transferred to Treasury and CIO.
- Credit costs: Q2 2023 included a net benefit (negative provision), versus a modest provision in Q2 2022; modest provision increase year-to-date.
- Expenses: Noninterest expense rose sharply to about $1.2 billion, driven by $562 million of costs from the First Republic acquisition, higher legal expense, and the absence of prior-year FX-related expense benefits.
- Segment breakdown:
  - Treasury and CIO delivered roughly $1.3 billion of Q2 revenue and $1.1 billion of net income.
  - Other Corporate delivered roughly $2.5 billion of Q2 revenue and $1.6 billion of net income.
- Balance sheet and other metrics:
  - Period-end assets down 13% year-over-year to about $1.26 trillion.
  - Deposits up 60% to about $21.1 billion, predominantly from international consumer initiatives.
  - Loans roughly flat.
  - Headcount up 12% to about 45,235.
- Notables/footnotes:
  - Results include impacts of the First Republic acquisition; related taxes are reflected in the bargain purchase gain (see Note 28).
  - Tax-equivalent adjustments from municipal bond income are included in total net revenue.

top5_chunks.title: Revenue
top5_chunks.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results of operations for 2022 versus 2021, with references to prior-year analysis and critical accounting estimates.
- Revenue overview: Presents a three-year revenue table (2020–2022) detailing noninterest revenue components and net interest income; total net revenue rose to $128.7B in 2022 (noninterest revenue $62.0B; net interest income $66.7B).
- Investment banking fees: Declined due to volatile markets leading to lower equity/debt underwriting and advisory activity in CIB.
- Principal transactions: Increased on strong Fixed Income Markets (notably Currencies & Emerging Markets and Rates) and Equity Derivatives/Prime Finance; partially offset by:
  - $836M loss in Credit Adjustments & Other (funding spread widening; Russia/commodities exposures),
  - Net markdowns on held-for-sale bridge financing positions (CIB and CB),
  - Higher losses on legacy private equity (Corporate),
  - Net losses in Treasury & CIO tied to cash deployment (offset by related NII).
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Up on higher service fee volume in CCB, mostly offset by greater client earnings credits reducing cash management fees in CB and CIB.
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Down due to lower AWM management fees (market declines), lower custody fees (Securities Services), and lower brokerage commissions; partially offset by higher travel-related and annuity commissions in CCB and reduced money market fund fee waivers plus net inflows.
- Investment securities gains/losses: Larger net losses from sales of MBS and U.S. Treasuries due to portfolio repositioning in Treasury & CIO.
- Mortgage fees and related income: Down on lower production margins and volumes; largely offset by higher servicing income (no prior-year MSR risk-management loss and more third-party loans serviced).
- Card income: Down due to higher amortization of new account origination costs; partly offset by higher annual fees and increased commercial card payments revenue in CIB and CB.
- Other income: Down on lower auto operating lease income and investment losses in CIB/AWM; offsets included a $914M gain on sale of Visa B shares, other investment gains, insurance settlement proceeds, a gain on an equity-method investment in CB, favorable FX impacts on net investment hedges (Treasury & CIO), and absence of prior-year weather-related write-downs.
- Net interest income: Increased on higher rates and loan growth, partially offset by lower Markets NII. Average interest-earning assets were ~$3.3T with a 2.78% yield; net yield 2.00% (up 36 bps); net yield excluding Markets 2.60% (up 69 bps).
- Notes: CIB Markets performance assessed on a total revenue basis; references provided to segment discussions, non-GAAP reconciliations, and detailed schedules.

top5_chunks.summary: JPMorgan Chase files a consolidated U.S. federal return and accounts for income taxes using the asset and liability method, recognizing deferred tax assets/liabilities for temporary differences at expected future tax rates and recording a valuation allowance as needed; significant judgment is required due to multi-jurisdictional complexity, and final tax positions may differ from current amounts. The effective tax rate reconciliations show rates of 18.4% (2022), 18.9% (2021), and 18.7% (2020) versus the 21% statutory rate, reflecting impacts from state and local taxes, tax‑exempt income, non‑U.S. earnings, business tax credits, and other items. Income tax expense totaled $8.49 billion in 2022, $11.23 billion in 2021, and $6.68 billion in 2020, comprising current expense of $11.23 billion, $7.48 billion, and $10.26 billion and deferred expense/(benefit) of $(2.74) billion, $3.75 billion, and $(3.57) billion, respectively; audit resolutions produced tax benefits/(expense) of $331 million (2022), $(69) million (2021), and $72 million (2020). Tax effects recorded directly in stockholders’ equity were a $4.5 billion decrease (2022), $2.0 billion increase (2021), and $827 million decrease (2020). Income before tax was U.S. $34.63B/$50.13B/$27.31B and non‑U.S. $11.54B/$9.44B/$8.50B for 2022/2021/2020; any U.S. tax on GILTI is recognized as incurred and was not material at December 31, 2022.
top5_chunks.text:
Income taxes  
JPMorgan Chase  and its eligible subsidiaries file a 
consolidated U.S. federal income tax return. JPMorgan 
Chase uses the asset and liability method to provi de for 
income taxes on all transactions recorded in the 
Consolidated Financial Statements. This method requires 
that income taxes reflect the expected future tax 
consequences of temporary differences between the 
carrying amounts of assets or liabilities for book and tax 
purposes. Accordingly, a deferred tax asset or liability for 
each temporary difference is determined based on the tax 
rates that the Firm expects to be in effect when the 
underlying items of income and expense are realized. 
JPMorgan Chase’s expense for income taxes includes the 
current and deferred portions of that expense. A valuation 
allowance is established to reduce deferred tax assets to 
the amount the Firm expects to realize.
Due to the inherent complexities arising from the nature of  
the Firm’s businesses, and from conducting business and 
being taxed in a substantial number of jurisdictions, 
significant judgments and estimates are required to be 
made. Agreement of tax liabilities between  JPMorgan Chase 
and the many tax jurisdictions in which  the Firm files tax 
returns may not be finalized for several years. Thus,  the 
Firm’s final tax-related assets and liabilities may ultimately 
be different from those currently reported.

top1_chunks.title: Outlook
top1_chunks.summary:
- Regulatory updates: In July 2023, U.S. banking regulators proposed Basel III “finalization” changes replacing the advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach (no internal models except for Market risk) and applying the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches. The rule would impact banks with assets of $100B+ (including U.S. GSIBs), with a proposed effective date of July 1, 2025 and a three-year transition. Separately, the Federal Reserve proposed revising the GSIB surcharge to an annual assessment based on averaged quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain inputs), reducing surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps, and making technical Method 2 amendments, effective two quarters after finalization.

- Outlook and disclosures: The document contains forward-looking statements subject to significant risks and uncertainties, with references to detailed risk factors and forward-looking statements sections. It notes that 2023 performance depends on macroeconomic, market, geopolitical, competitive, client activity, and regulatory developments, and that the firm will adjust operations as conditions evolve.

- FDIC special assessment: The FDIC proposed a special assessment (12.5 bps annual rate) on estimated uninsured deposits as of December 31, 2022, to recover DIF losses tied to March 12, 2023 systemic risk actions. If finalized as proposed, JPMorgan Chase expects to record approximately $3B pre-tax expense in the quarter of finalization, anticipated in 2H 2023.

- 2023 guidance: Management expects full-year net interest income and net interest income excluding Markets to be approximately $87B (market dependent), adjusted expense to be approximately $84.5B (market dependent and excluding any FDIC special assessment), and a Card Services net charge-off rate of about 2.6%. Certain figures are non-GAAP, with references to reconciliation pages.

top5_chunks.title: Outlook
top5_chunks.summary:
- Regulatory updates: In July 2023, U.S. banking regulators proposed Basel III “finalization” changes replacing the advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach (no internal models except for Market risk) and applying the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches. The rule would impact banks with assets of $100B+ (including U.S. GSIBs), with a proposed effective date of July 1, 2025 and a three-year transition. Separately, the Federal Reserve proposed revising the GSIB surcharge to an annual assessment based on averaged quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain inputs), reducing surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps, and making technical Method 2 amendments, effective two quarters after finalization.

- Outlook and disclosures: The document contains forward-looking statements subject to significant risks and uncertainties, with references to detailed risk factors and forward-looking statements sections. It notes that 2023 performance depends on macroeconomic, market, geopolitical, competitive, client activity, and regulatory developments, and that the firm will adjust operations as conditions evolve.

- FDIC special assessment: The FDIC proposed a special assessment (12.5 bps annual rate) on estimated uninsured deposits as of December 31, 2022, to recover DIF losses tied to March 12, 2023 systemic risk actions. If finalized as proposed, JPMorgan Chase expects to record approximately $3B pre-tax expense in the quarter of finalization, anticipated in 2H 2023.

- 2023 guidance: Management expects full-year net interest income and net interest income excluding Markets to be approximately $87B (market dependent), adjusted expense to be approximately $84.5B (market dependent and excluding any FDIC special assessment), and a Card Services net charge-off rate of about 2.6%. Certain figures are non-GAAP, with references to reconciliation pages.

top5_chunks.title: Firmwide overview
top5_chunks.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for the second quarter of 2023; directs readers to the full Form 10‑Q and 2022 Form 10‑K for complete trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Headline results (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022): net income up 67% to $14.5B; EPS $4.75; ROE 20%; ROTCE 25%.
- Revenue: total net revenue up 34% to $41.3B, driven by:
  - Net interest income up 44% to $21.8B on higher rates and, to a lesser extent, the First Republic acquisition; NII excluding Markets up 63% to $22.4B.
  - Noninterest revenue up 25% to $19.5B, reflecting the First Republic bargain purchase gain of ~$2.7B (Corporate) and stronger Markets NIR, partially offset by ~$900M of investment securities losses in Treasury and CIO.
  - Markets revenue declined, with lower Markets NII largely offset by higher Markets NIR.
- Expenses: noninterest expense up 11% to $20.8B, driven by higher compensation (headcount and wage inflation), ~$599M of First Republic–related expense, increased technology and marketing investments, and higher legal expense.
- Credit costs: provision for credit losses of $2.9B, including a $1.5B net ACL build and $1.4B of net charge-offs.
  - ACL build includes ~$1.2B to establish allowance for First Republic loans and commitments; additional builds in Card Services and wholesale (CB) largely offset by a reduction in Corporate.
  - Net charge-offs rose, mainly in Card, as 30+ day delinquencies normalized to pre‑pandemic levels.
- Allowance and asset quality: total ACL $24.3B; allowance-to-loans coverage ratio 1.75% (vs. 1.69% prior year); nonperforming assets ~$7.8B, flat year-over-year with mix shift toward wholesale nonaccruals.
- Balance sheet trends: firmwide average loans up 13% to ~$1.2T (CCB and CB, including First Republic); firmwide average deposits down 6% to ~$2.4T due to AWM migration to higher‑yielding investments, attrition in CIB/CB (including deliberate reductions), and higher CCB spending, partially offset by First Republic inflows in CCB and Corporate increases tied to international consumer initiatives.
- Capital and liquidity:
  - CET1 capital ~$236B; Standardized CET1 ratio 13.8% and Advanced CET1 ratio 13.9% (reflecting CECL transition); Tier 1 15.4%; Total capital 17.3%; SLR 5.8%.
  - Tangible book value per share $79.90 (up 15%); book value per share $98.11 (up 14%).
  - Liquidity: HQLA ~$792B and unencumbered marketable securities ~$620B, totaling ~ $1.4T of liquidity sources.
- Additional context:
  - Pre-provision profit up 71% to $20.5B.
  - Managed basis total net revenue $42.4B; Markets revenue $7.0B; memo metrics provided for NII/NIR excluding Markets.
  - Non-GAAP measures cited include pre-provision profit, ROTCE, TCE, TBVPS, NII/NIR excluding Markets, and managed-basis revenue; reconciliations referenced in the MD&A.
  - Comparisons are Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022; references provided to sections on capital, liquidity, consolidated results, business segment results, and First Republic acquisition details.

top5_chunks.title: Contract assets
top5_chunks.summary:
- Research and development costs: Distinguishes company-funded (IR&D) vs customer-funded R&D; both expensed to cost of sales as incurred. Company-funded R&D is allocated to contracts via G&A and generally recoverable on U.S. Government contracts; customer-funded R&D is charged directly. Company-funded R&D expense: $1.5B (2021), $1.3B (2020, 2019).
- Stock-based compensation: Grants RSUs and PSUs that generally vest over three years. Fair value measured at grant (RSUs at market price less dividend discount; PSUs either similarly or via Monte Carlo for market conditions). Expense recognized ratably over requisite service/vesting periods, with adjustments for forfeitures and performance-based PSU vesting expectations; retirement eligibility can shorten requisite service.
- Income taxes: Uses asset/liability method for deferred taxes based on enacted rates. Uncertain tax positions evaluated under more-likely-than-not threshold; recognizes largest benefit likely to be realized; interest/penalties recorded in income tax expense (not material). State/local income and franchise taxes are allowable/allocable to government contracts and recorded in operating costs; changes in deferred state taxes/unrecognized benefits recognized in unallocated corporate expenses.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Highly liquid instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
- Receivables: Unconditional right to consideration, recorded net of expected credit losses; no significant impairments in 2019–2021.
- Contract assets: Unbilled amounts from percentage-of-completion (cost-to-cost) when revenue recognized exceeds billings; recorded at amounts expected to be billed/collected; classified as current based on operating cycle even if billed/collected beyond one year.
- Inventories: Lower of cost or net realizable value; primarily work-in-process (labor, materials, subcontractor, overhead). Pre-contract costs capitalized when directly related to a specifically identifiable probable contract, generate/enhance resources, and are recoverable; otherwise expensed. Materials/spares use FIFO or average cost. Write-downs recorded when not recoverable or utility diminishes.
- Contract liabilities: Advance payments and billings in excess of revenue; classified as current based on operating cycle; reported net by contract.
- Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost; depreciation accelerated in first half of life then straight-line thereafter; useful lives: buildings 10–40 years, machinery/equipment 5–15 years; no depreciation on construction in progress. Depreciation expense: $904M (2021), $853M (2020), $794M (2019). Long-lived assets reviewed for impairment; write down to fair value if undiscounted cash flows are less than carrying amount.
- Capitalized software: Certain internal-use software costs capitalized and amortized straight-line over 2–6 years; no amortization until ready for use. Net balances: $777M (2021) and $686M (2020), with accumulated amortization of $2.3B and $2.2B; amortization expense: $175M (2021), $166M (2020), $111M (2019).
- Fair value measurements: Defines hierarchy—Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (observable inputs other than quoted prices), Level 3 (significant unobservable inputs).
- Investments: Primarily assets in a trust for non-qualified deferred compensation plans, recorded in other noncurrent assets; fair value $2.1B (2021) and $2.0B (2020). Net gains: $205M (2021), $231M (2020), $233M (2019), recognized in other unallocated, net within cost of sales. Lockheed Martin Ventures strategic investments include equity and convertible instruments; most measured at cost with adjustments for observable price changes or impairment; Level 1 securities at fair value.
top5_chunks.text:
Contract assets include unbilled amounts typically resulting from sales under contracts when the percentage-of-completion cost-to-cost method of
revenue recognition is utilized and revenue recognized exceeds the amount billed to the customer. Contract assets are recorded at the net amount expected to be billed and
collected. Contract assets are classified as current based on our contract operating cycle, and include amounts that may be billed and collected beyond one year due to the
long-cycle nature of our contracts.

top5_chunks.title: Capitalized software
top5_chunks.summary:

Pre-contract costs are capitalized as WIP when directly related to a specifically identifiable probable contract, create/enhance resources for performance, and are recoverable; recognized in cost of sales upon contract award and transfer of goods/services. Other pre-contract and start-up costs are expensed as incurred. Materials/spares use FIFO or average cost. Losses recognized for unrecoverable pre-contract costs or diminished inventory utility.
- Contract liabilities: Include advances and billings in excess of recognized revenue; classified as current based on contract operating cycle and presented net of recognized revenue on a contract-by-contract basis.
- Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost; depreciated using accelerated methods in first half of useful life then straight-line thereafter. Useful lives: buildings 10–40 years; machinery/equipment 5–15 years. No depreciation on construction in progress. Depreciation expense: $904M (2021), $853M (2020), $794M (2019). - Capitalized software: Internal-use software costs capitalized in other noncurrent assets; amortized straight-line over 2–6 years starting when ready for intended use. Net balances: $777M (2021) and $686M (2020), with accumulated amortization of $2.3B and $2.2B, respectively. Amortization expense: $175M (2021), $166M (2020), $111M (2019).
- Fair value of financial instruments: Measured using a three-level hierarchy—Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (other observable inputs), Level 3 (significant unobservable inputs).
- Investments: Primarily assets in a trust for non-qualified deferred compensation plans measured at fair value and reported in other noncurrent assets; balances of $2.1B (2021) and $2.0B (2020). Net gains of $205M (2021), $231M (2020), $233M (2019), recognized in other unallocated, net within cost of sales to align with related liabilities. Through Lockheed Martin Ventures, strategic investments in early-stage technology companies are made via equity, warrants, convertible debt, or funds; most lack readily determinable fair values and are carried at cost adjusted for observable price changes or impairment, while Level 1 investments are recorded at fair value.
top5_chunks.text:
Capitalized software – We capitalize certain costs associated with the development or purchase of internal-use software. The amounts capitalized are included in other
noncurrent assets on our consolidated balance sheets and are amortized on a straight-line basis over the estimated useful life of the resulting software, which ranges from
two to six years. As of December 31, 2021 and 2020, capitalized software totaled $777 million and $686 million, net of accumulated amortization of $2.3 billion and
$2.2 billion. No amortization expense is recorded until the software is ready for its intended use. Amortization expense related to capitalized software was $175 million in
2021, $166 million in 2020 and $111 million in 2019.

top5_chunks.title: Investments
top5_chunks.summary:
- Inventories: Carried at lower of cost or estimated net realizable value. Majority is work-in-process (labor, material, subcontractor, overhead) for contracts where control hasn’t transferred. Pre-contract costs are capitalized as WIP only if tied to an identifiable probable award, directly related to the contract, create/enhance resources for performance, and are recoverable; expensed upon transfer of products/services after award. Other pre-contract and start-up costs are expensed as incurred. Other inventory (materials, spares, supplies) uses FIFO or average cost. Losses recognized for nonrecoverable pre-contract costs or diminished utility (damage, obsolescence, price changes).
- Contract liabilities: Advance payments and billings in excess of recognized revenue; classified as current based on contract operating cycle and presented net of revenue recognized on a contract-by-contract basis at period end.
- Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost; accelerated depreciation in first half of useful life then straight-line thereafter. Useful lives: buildings 10–40 years; machinery/equipment 5–15 years. No depreciation on construction in progress. Depreciation expense: $904m (2021), $853m (2020), $794m (2019). Long-lived assets reviewed for impairment based on undiscounted cash flows; write down to fair value if impaired.
- Capitalized software: Internal-use software costs capitalized in other noncurrent assets; amortized straight-line over 2–6 years once ready for intended use. Net balances: $777m (2021) and $686m (2020); accumulated amortization $2.3b (2021) and $2.2b (2020). Amortization expense: $175m (2021), $166m (2020), $111m (2019).
- Fair value measurements: Uses observable and unobservable inputs with a three-level hierarchy—Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (other observable inputs), Level 3 (significant unobservable inputs).
- Investments (deferred compensation trust): Substantially all fair value assets fund non-qualified deferred compensation liabilities; fair value $2.1b (2021) and $2.0b (2020) in other noncurrent assets. Net gains of $205m (2021), $231m (2020), $233m (2019), recorded in cost of sales (other unallocated, net) to align with plan liabilities.
- Lockheed Martin Ventures Fund: Strategic early-stage investments (equity, warrants, convertible debt, funds). Most measured at cost adjusted for observable price changes or impairment; Level 1 at fair value each period. Carrying amounts: $465m (2021) and $173m (2020) in other assets (current and noncurrent). 2021 net gains $265m ($199m after-tax, $0.72/share) in other non-operating income, net; no net gains in 2020.
- Equity method investments: Applied where significant influence (generally 20%–50% ownership); carried in other noncurrent assets. Share of investee results recorded in operating profit within other income, net. Impairment recognized for other-than-temporary declines. Balances: $689m (2021) and $784m (2020), primarily United Launch Alliance. Share of net earnings: $97m (2021), $163m (2020), $154m (2019); Space segment included approx. $67m, $135m, and $145m, respectively. AMMROC stake sale: agreement in July 2020 for $307m; recognized $128m noncash impairment ($96m after-tax, $0.34/share) in 2020; sale completed Nov 25, 2020 with full cash proceeds.
- Goodwill and intangible assets: Acquisitions recorded at fair value. Goodwill is excess over identifiable net assets; intangible assets include customer programs, trademarks, customer relationships, technology, etc., amortized over 5–20 years. Goodwill balance $10.8b at Dec 31, 2021 and 2020. Goodwill tested at the reporting unit level at least annually (Q4) or upon triggering events, using qualitative screening or quantitative testing. Quantitative tests rely on DCF and market-based methods (comparable companies and transactions), requiring judgments on future cash flows, growth, discount rates, and valuation multiples, considering market conditions, U.S. Government budgets, orders, supplier contracts, and labor agreements.
top5_chunks.text:
Investments – Substantially all assets measured at fair value represent investments held in a separate trust to fund certain of our non-qualified deferred compensation
plan liabilities. As of December 31, 2021 and 2020, the fair value of our investments held in trust totaled $2.1 billion and $2.0 billion and was included in other noncurrent
assets on our consolidated balance sheets.
Net gains on these securities were $205 million, $231 million and $233 million in 2021, 2020 and 2019. Gains and losses on these investments are included in other
unallocated, net within cost of sales on our consolidated statements of earnings in order to align the classification of changes in the market value of investments held for the
plan with changes in the value of the corresponding plan liabilities.
Additionally, through our Lockheed Martin Ventures Fund, we make strategic investments in certain early stage companies that we believe are advancing or developing
new technologies applicable to our business. These investments may be in the form of common or preferred stock, warrants, convertible debt securities or investments in
funds. Most of the investments are in equity securities without readily determinable fair values, which are measured initially at cost and are then adjusted to fair value only
if there is an observable price change or reduced for impairment, if applicable. Investments with quoted market prices in active markets (Level 1) are recorded at fair value
at the end of each reporting period. The carrying amounts of investments

held in our Lockheed Martin Ventures Fund were $465 million and $173 million at December 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020 and are included on our consolidated
balance sheets within other assets, both current and noncurrent. During 2021, we recorded $265 million ($199 million, or $0.72 per share, after-tax) of net gains, compared
to recording no net gains during 2020, due to changes in fair value and/or sales of investments which are reflected in the other non-operating income, net account on our

top5_chunks.title: Goodwill and Intangible Assets
top5_chunks.summary:
- Fair value investments: Lockheed Martin Ventures Fund holdings were $465 million (2021) and $173 million (2020), recorded in other assets. In 2021, the company recognized $265 million of net gains ($199 million after-tax; $0.72 per share) from fair value changes/sales, reported in other non-operating income, net; no gains in 2020.
- Equity method investments: Used for holdings with significant influence (generally 20%–50% ownership), recorded in other noncurrent assets; share of investee results recognized in operating profit within other income, net. Balances totaled $689 million (2021) and $784 million (2020), primarily United Launch Alliance (ULA). Share of net earnings was $97 million (2021), $163 million (2020), and $154 million (2019), with approximately $67 million, $135 million, and $145 million, respectively, in the Space segment. The company recorded a $128 million noncash impairment ($96 million after-tax; $0.34 per share) in 2020 tied to the sale of its AMMROC interest for $307 million, completed November 25, 2020.
- Goodwill and intangible assets: Business combinations recorded at fair value; goodwill reflects excess purchase price; identifiable intangibles include customer programs, relationships, trademarks, and technology, amortized over 5–20 years. Goodwill was $10.8 billion at December 31, 2021 and 2020. The company performs annual (Q4) or trigger-based goodwill impairment tests using qualitative or quantitative methods; quantitative tests use DCF and market approaches with judgments about cash flows, growth, discount rates (WACC), and market multiples. No goodwill impairments were identified in 2019–2021. Indefinite-lived intangibles are tested annually (not amortized); finite-lived intangibles are amortized 5–20 years and tested upon indicators of impairment.
- Leases: Predominantly long-term operating leases; right-of-use (ROU) assets recorded in other noncurrent assets; lease liabilities in other current/noncurrent liabilities. Both measured at the present value of lease payments using the company’s incremental borrowing rate when no implicit rate exists. Options to extend/terminate included when reasonably certain; expense recognized straight-line in cost of sales. Lease and non-lease components are combined; a portfolio approach is applied for certain equipment; ROU assets are tested for impairment consistent with PPE policy.
- Postretirement benefit plans: Defined benefit pensions, retiree medical/life, and other postemployment benefits measured via actuarial valuations using key assumptions (discount rate, expected long-term asset returns, mortality, health care cost trends, turnover). Asset gains/losses are smoothed over three years to determine market-related value; corridor method amortizes amounts exceeding 10% of the greater of plan assets or obligations. Funded status (fair value of assets minus benefit obligation) is recognized on the balance sheet as a noncurrent asset or liability under GAAP; ERISA funded status is determined on a different basis.
top5_chunks.text:
Goodwill and Intangible Assets – The assets and liabilities of acquired businesses are recorded under the acquisition method of accounting at their estimated fair
values at the date of acquisition. Goodwill represents costs in excess of fair values assigned to the underlying identifiable net assets of acquired businesses. Intangible assets
from acquired businesses are recognized at fair value on the acquisition date and consist of customer programs, trademarks, customer relationships, technology and other
intangible assets. Customer programs include values assigned to major programs of acquired businesses and represent the aggregate value associated with the customer
relationships, contracts, technology and trademarks underlying the associated program. Intangible assets are amortized over a period of expected cash flows used to
measure fair value, which ranges from five to 20 years.
Our goodwill balance was $10.8 billion at both December 31, 2021 and 2020. We perform an impairment test of our goodwill at least annually in the fourth quarter or
more frequently whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying value of goodwill may be impaired. Such events or changes in circumstances may
include a significant deterioration in overall economic conditions, changes in the business climate of our industry, a decline in our market capitalization, operating
performance indicators, competition, reorganizations of our business, U.S. Government budget restrictions or the disposal of all or a portion of a reporting unit. Our
goodwill has been allocated to and is tested for impairment at a level referred to as the reporting unit, which is our business segment level or a level below the business
segment. The level at which we test goodwill for impairment requires us to determine whether the operations below the business segment constitute a self-sustaining
business for which discrete financial information is available and segment management regularly reviews the operating results.
We may use either a qualitative or quantitative approach when testing a reporting unit’s goodwill for impairment. For selected reporting units where we use the
qualitative approach, we perform a qualitative evaluation of events and circumstances impacting the reporting unit to determine the likelihood of goodwill impairment.
Based on that qualitative evaluation, if we determine it is more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit exceeds its carrying amount, no further evaluation is
necessary. Otherwise we perform a quantitative impairment test. We perform quantitative tests for most reporting units at least once every three years. However, for certain
reporting units we may perform a quantitative impairment test every year.
For the quantitative impairment test we compare the fair value of a reporting unit to its carrying value, including goodwill. If the fair value of a reporting unit exceeds
its carrying value, goodwill of the reporting unit is not impaired. If the carrying value of the reporting unit, including goodwill, exceeds its fair value, a goodwill
impairment loss is recognized in an amount equal to that excess. We generally estimate the fair value of each reporting unit using a combination of a discounted cash flow
(DCF) analysis and market-based valuation methodologies such as comparable public company trading values and values observed in recent business acquisitions.
Determining fair value requires the exercise of significant judgments, including the amount and timing of expected future cash flows, long-term growth rates, discount rates
and relevant comparable public company earnings multiples and relevant transaction multiples. The cash flows employed in the DCF analysis are based on our best
estimate of future sales, earnings and cash flows after considering factors such as general market conditions, U.S. Government budgets, existing firm orders, expected
future orders, contracts with suppliers, labor agreements, changes in
77Table of Contents
working capital, long term business plans and recent operating performance. The discount rates utilized in the DCF analysis are based on the respective reporting unit’s
weighted average cost of capital, which takes into account the relative weights of each component of capital structure (equity and debt) and represents the expected cost of
new capital, adjusted as appropriate to consider the risk inherent in future cash flows of the respective reporting unit. The carrying value of each reporting unit includes the
assets and liabilities employed in its operations, goodwill and allocations of certain assets and liabilities held at the business segment and corporate levels.
During the fourth quarters of 2021, 2020 and 2019, we performed our annual goodwill impairment test for each of our reporting units. The results of our annual
impairment tests of goodwill indicated that no impairment existed.
Acquired intangible assets deemed to have indefinite lives are not amortized, but are subject to annual impairment testing. This testing compares carrying value to fair
value and, when appropriate, the carrying value of these assets is reduced to fair value. Finite-lived intangibles are amortized to expense over the applicable useful lives,
ranging from five to 20 years, based on the nature of the asset and the underlying pattern of economic benefit as reflected by future net cash inflows. We perform an
impairment test of finite-lived intangibles whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate their carrying value may be impaired.

intangible assets, investments and other assets for impairment; income taxes including deferred income taxes; fair value measurements; and contingencies.
